name: Tsaxur
confidence_why: Schulze 1997 and Talibov 2001 describe a dynamic accent that falls on the second syllable of nouns but on the first syllable of verbs, whereas Kodzasov's phonetic study of the Mikik variety (Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990), built on an accented dictionary, finds no word stress at all but a syllable-tone contrast on the first two syllables, so both the type of system and the strict second-syllable placement are contested.

tone_statements.quote: Kibrik & Kodzasov (1990: 344) describe Mikik Tsakhur as having four tones: gat͡ʃ (H) ‘horn’, ͡tʃiː (L) ‘dew’, t’ub (R) ‘finger’, wok (F) ‘pig’. The tones are contrastive only on the first two syllables, with subsequent syllables subject to tonal neutralization. … Attested tonal combinations include: HH, LL, HL, LH, RR, RL, FH. Final sonorants can carry their own tone, and long vowels can carry two tones: zej (RL) ‘urine’, ͡tʃ’er (HL) ‘hair’; weːɣ (RL) ‘part of stomach’.

tone_statements.quote: Undoubtedly, stress in Lezgian languages is a result of metrical evolution. Data of more distant mountain languages give evidence of this. Thus, in Tsakhur stress did not become a common metrical property of word. Most words have no metrical head and display only a slight prominence of heavy syllables. It is noteworthy that those stress words which designate people and animals lose stress when they accomplish the semantic role of Patience. Other isolated mountain languages of this group (Budukh and Kryz) has no stress at all. Probably, they have syllabic tones but their word prosody needs a further study.
tone_statements.n_tones: None claimed for Tsakhur in this work (tones suggested only for Budukh/Kryz)

audit.recode_to: conflict (stress tradition: dynamic accent predominantly on 2nd syllable, verbs initial — Talibov 2001:421, Schulze 1997:22, Ibragimov 1990; vs. Kodzasov 1990:344 'словесное ударение отсутствует', 4 syllabic/moraic tones contrastive on the first two syllables). If the catalog prefers to keep a stress code pending Elementy 1999, downgrade fixed-strict -> fixed-dominant (2nd syllable; Talibov 'преимущественно', initial stress in verbs per Schulze) and add Kodzasov 1990 to 'contra'.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding quotations (Schulze 1997:22 §2.1.5; Talibov 2001:421 §2.1.2) confirmed verbatim in held page scan. (2) Deciding sources are two sketches (1997, 2001). They do not themselves support 'strict': Talibov says stress falls 'predominantly' on the 2nd syllable and can be initial (óхьанас, óкIанас); Schulze says verbs are always initial-stressed and CVC/CVRC monosyllabic nouns keep stem stress before suffixes. (3) downloaded now from the official MSU Kibrik site: Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990, where the phonetician Kodzasov, from fieldwork with an accentuated dictionary, states for Tsakhur (Mikik) 'word stress is absent' and describes four syllabic tones (H 137, L 33, R 26, F 11 monosyllables) contrastive only on the first two syllables (p.344), listing Tsakhur among the syllabic-tone languages of Daghestan (p.318). Schulze 1997 fn.33 knows of and rejects functional tone b

sources.quote: § 13. В цахурском языке ударение слабое, динамическое. Фиксируется оно на определенном слоге слова, но иногда имеет место перемещения от одного слога на другой. Вукӏу́л' 'голова', ген. (IV) вукӏуле́н > вукӏле́н. Долгие гласные всегда ударные: за́лым 'жестокий', а́зыр 'тысяча', ацӏа́л' 'знания'.
sources.note: The sketch calls stress weak and dynamic, 'fixed on a certain syllable' without naming which, with occasional shifts under inflection (вукӏу́л' 'head' > gen. вукӏуле́н > вукӏле́н; the same pair is given on p. 508 as vowel reduction tied to stress). Weight: 'long vowels are always stressed' (за́лым, а́зыр = first syllable; ацӏа́л' = second). Headwords in the dictionary carry an acute stress mark (preface p. 14: 'Заглавные слова сопровождаются ударением (вопрос в цахурском языке архисложный..'); sampled headwords: p. 20 Ава́з, Ава́л, Ава́лна, Ава́р, Ава́ра (all second syllable); p. 120 Г'и́чӏе

sources.quote: §4. Ударение — малоразработанный раздел цахурской фонетики. Предварительные данные позволяют констатировать, что для цахурского языка характерно силовое ударение. Ударение преимущественно падает на второй слог от начала слова (хьунйилие ‘женщина’, гиней ‘хлеб’), но может падать на первый (бхьанас ‘есть’, бкТанас ‘писать’), на третий ит. д. В мьогосложных словах кроме главного ударения может быть и побочное, например в хъёпалас ‘звать’ главное ударение падает на долгий г, побочное ударение — на второй слог.
sources.locator: Talibov 1967, book p. 593, Фонетика §4; stress shift with pre-tonic reduction in §5, same page
sources.note: Talibov calls stress 'силовое' (dynamic) and says it falls PREDOMINANTLY on the second syllable from the word beginning, matching the catalog second stress — but he does not call it fixed: it may fall on the first (бхьанас 'to eat', бкТанас 'to write') or third syllable, so the catalog kind 'fixed' is softened to a predominant second-syllable pattern with lexical exceptions. sources.citation: Kodzasov, Sandro V. 2003. Towards an evolutionary typology of stress. In: Proceedings of the 15th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (15th ICPhS), Barcelona 2003, pp. 63-66. ISBN 1-876346-48-5.
sources.quote: Undoubtedly, stress in Lezgian languages is a result of metrical evolution. Data of more distant mountain languages give evidence of this. Thus, in Tsakhur stress did not become a common metrical property of word. Most words have no metrical head and display only a slight prominence of heavy syllables. It is noteworthy that those stress words which designate people and animals lose stress when they accomplish the semantic role of Patience. Other isolated mountain languages of this group (Budukh and Kryz) has no stress at all. Probably, they have syllabic tones but their word prosody needs a further study.
sources.note: Kodzasov's late first-hand position: Tsakhur has no general word stress ('most words have no metrical head', only slight prominence of heavy syllables; a lexical class of stressed animate nouns loses stress in Patient role). He assigns 'probably syllabic tones' to Budukh and Kryz but makes NO tone claim for Tsakhur here - i.e. by 2003 he no longer presents Tsakhur as a tone language (contrast Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990 'four syllabic tones', the statement listed here). Short typological paper, no F0 data shown.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 15th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (15th ICPhS), Barcelona 2003

sources.note: Dedicated first-hand study of word stress in Tsakhur and Rutul. Secondhand via Borise 2018 (lingbuzz 004203 p. 21): 'According to yet another view, there is an overall tendency to fix stress in Tsakhur on the penult (Jeiranishvili 1964: 352; 1983: 95)' - i.e. a penult-stress analysis competing with the 2nd-syllable (Talibov/Ibragimov) and weight-based strong/weak-stress (Kodzasov 1999) accounts; no tone analysis expected (1964).
